opener.heading: Week 31: Camping Adventures ⛺
about: Camp goes up in the yard on Friday and stays up until Thursday. A sheet over the clothesline, a ring of stones with a paper fire inside it, four bedrolls, and a flag she paints herself. Every day adds one piece and every piece stays outside, so the thing she walks out to on Thursday morning is one she has been living in for a week.

The week crosses from July into August and half of it runs on water: two bowls of dishwashing out by the tent, a soapy shower curtain down the lawn, a dish put out for the birds in the heat. Thursday is the big day. Everything still living indoors goes out to the tent in one morning, she finishes the camp, and the whole thing comes down after lunch while everybody still likes it. You spend Wednesday getting it ready, and Wednesday is the half she will ask to do again.
azlyn: Pegs, weights and ties. What holds a sheet up in a breeze, and what lets it go.
A camp has an order. It goes up in a sequence, gets lived in, and comes down in that sequence backwards.
One symbol, one meaning. She paints a flag and then reads it from thirty feet away, which is the same trick letters run on.
Real kitchen work. Snapping beans, folding a foil seam, levelling off a cup, counting spoons out loud and starting again when she loses the number.
Staying still outdoors. Twenty minutes on her back naming what she can hear, which is harder for her than any of the building.
you: A space she can fit inside changes the way she plays in it
Fever makes children clingy, and meeting it is the fastest way through the day
Naming a sound is how she learns to pick it out of the rest
Summer needs less structure than you'd think
Symbols are a big abstraction, and flags are the easiest entry point
A list she can read herself puts her in charge of the packing
Big days are frequently too big, and the fix is leaving early
shopping: An old flat sheet or a double duvet cover
Heavy stones or bricks, about 25 (off the wall or out of the garden)
Tent pegs, or 4 straight sticks for the corners
Sticks for the fire, 15 to 30, gathered on Friday's walk
A garden cane, bamboo pole or broom handle
An old shower curtain, tarpaulin or heavy plastic sheet (two split trash bags taped together does a short one)
A pair of adult scissors (adult only)
Thick card, 6 sheets (twelve strips and four luggage labels)
A hardback book or a piece of stiff card for a drawing board
Red, orange and yellow paper (junk mail, a magazine or a grocery bag)
An old white pillowcase, dish towel or plain t-shirt for the flag
A flashlight with fresh batteries, and a spare set
Clean jam jars or small lidded tubs, 6
Green beans, plus zucchini or sweetcorn
A scrubbing brush and a sponge
A washcloth and a damp cloth
A saucepan lid and a wooden spoon, for the camp bell
A dustpan and brush, or a stiff yard broom
A pitcher, and 3 cups with lids
Blankets or large towels, 4, one per person for the bedrolls
An old blanket for the ground
An old towel or picnic blanket for the tent floor, and a rug for Thursday
A low bench, an upturned crate or a step
Two chairs to string a short line between
A wide shallow dish or an old trash can lid for the birds
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 13 months this week. He walks, climbs anything knee-high and would rather carry something across the yard than sit down with it. He turns 14 months on Thursday the 5th, and brings scribbles, two blocks stacked, and three to five words you can make out.

days.title: The Tent Goes Up
days.prepTonight: Dig out an old flat sheet, the clothespins and a bucket of stones by the back door, and parboil four potatoes for tomorrow's parcels.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Cool Bath and a Camping Book

opening.title: Clearing the Ground
opening.need: 1 stiff yard broom · 1 bucket · 4 sticks or tent pegs.
steps: Walk the garden with her and let her choose where camp goes. Two things decide it: flat ground and shade by midday.
Sweep the loose stuff into a pile and let her pick it into the bucket. Run your flat hand over the square afterwards for the stones she missed.
Push a stick into each corner. That patch is camp now, and the sheet goes over it at quarter past nine.

main.title: The Clothesline Tent
materials: 1 old flat sheet or a double duvet cover
The clothesline, or rope tied between a fence and a tree
1 old towel or picnic blanket for the floor
The 4 corner sticks from this morning
steps: Throw the sheet over the line and slide it along until both sides hang the same.
Clip the sheet to the line, one peg every hand's width, eight or ten in all. Every peg goes over line and sheet together.
Weight both long edges from the outside with the stones, spaced along the hem so the walls hang straight. Nothing goes on the roof.
Cut the string into four eighteen-inch lengths with your scissors and tie a corner at each end out to a corner stick, so both doorways stand open.
Lay the towel or picnic blanket inside, corner to corner, and send her in.
Have her crawl the length twice, in one door and out the other. Anything she brings down gets rebuilt before you call it finished.
main.tip: Pitch it lower than you think you need to. A sheet at your shoulder sags to her head by lunchtime.

outside.title: The Firewood Walk
paras: Take a bag to the hedge at the end of the road and gather sticks for a fire nobody will light. Dry ones, thumb-thick and shorter than her arm. Fifteen is enough, thirty is better. She carries the bag home.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and walking. Give him one stick of his own, because holding something while moving is the job he is on now. He drops it, stops, picks it up and sets off again. That is the pace for the last hundred yards.

second.title: The Paper Campfire
second.intro: Camp needs a fire. Stones, sticks, torn paper and a flashlight, outside the tent door all week.
materials: Red, orange and yellow paper (junk mail, a magazine, or a grocery bag torn into strips)
1 empty tin or a small plastic tub to stand the flashlight in
steps: Lay the stones in a ring the size of a bike wheel, a long stride out from the tent door. She places every one.
Stand three sticks against each other like a tripod and lean the rest around them. It falls over. Build it again and let her work out that the first three hold the rest up.
Tear the paper into flames a hand long, twenty or so, and twist the bottom of each one into a stalk.
Tape the stalks low on the sticks so the flames stand upright between them, red near the ground and yellow at the top. Tape paper to stick, never paper to paper.
Stand the tin in the middle of the stack and drop the flashlight into it pointing straight up.
Switch it on and kneel in the doorway to look at the fire from inside, where the shade lets the light show.

Leave it built. At quarter past four, lift the flashlight out of the tin and take her into the tent with it, then untie the four corner strings so both doorways fall shut. A sheet with the doors down is as dark as July gets.
second.tip: Give the fire one rule and hold it all week: the sticks stay inside the ring.

alternatives: Sticks in the ring and no paper flames at all.
Sort the firewood into three piles by length and stop there.
Build the fire indoors on a tray and put the tent up tomorrow.
outAgain: A friend's house, and take the flashlight, because she describes a tent better with a prop in her hand
Your own street at half past two, walking the shady side on purpose
The paddling pool in the yard, if leaving camp is more than anyone can face
The playground with the tunnel, which she will be calling a tent by now

aroundWorld.title: Norway: Allemannsretten ⛺
paras: Norwegian law gives everybody the right to roam. Anyone can walk open country, swim in the lakes, pick berries and pitch a tent for a night on land they do not own, so long as they stay about five hundred feet from the nearest house and leave the ground as they found it.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Make a matpakke, the Norwegian packed lunch: open sandwiches stacked with a square of parchment paper between each one and eaten outside. Azlyn builds the pile and wraps it.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Norwegian nurseries take the children out in every weather, and some spend the whole day outdoors.

days.krestonPM: At 13 months he climbs, and a knee-high ring of stones reads as an invitation. Give him two stones of his own, each wider than his fist and too big for his mouth, to carry from the wall to the ring and back. Sit him in the doorway with the flashlight switched off, then take it back before the fire goes together.

insight.headline: A space she can fit inside changes the way she plays in it.
paras: Azlyn has been climbing into cupboards and under the table since she was two, and a sheet over the clothesline gives her the same thing with a door on it. A small enclosure does two jobs at once. It cuts the amount of room her attention has to cover, so the play she starts in there runs longer and gets more complicated than the same play on open carpet. It also hands her a boundary she controls, which is why the first thing out of her mouth is who is allowed in. Children with a den of some kind take themselves back to it when they are tired or cross, and settle there before anyone suggests it.

days.safety: A clothesline sits at her neck height and a rope between two trees sits lower. The sheet stays on it all week, so peg something bright along any bare stretch she runs past. Kreston is 13 months, walks straight at anything new and pulls on it, so nothing heavy sits where it can come down on him. Every stone you hand him is wider than his own fist and too big for his mouth, and the ring stones stay in the ring. Weight the sheet from the outside and keep the roof clear. The build and the stick walk are both outdoors before noon, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Camp Kitchen
days.prepTonight: The potatoes are boiled and cold in the fridge. Cut eight eighteen-inch lengths of string and four luggage labels out of thick card for this afternoon, and stand the foil and the baking tray on the side.

opening.title: Snapping the Beans
opening.need: a bag of green beans · 2 bowls · 1 low step or upturned crate.
steps: Sit her on the step in the shade with the full bowl on her lap and the empty one beside her.
Show her the snap once. Hold a bean at both ends, bend it until it goes, then break each half again.
Leave her to it and go and get the foil out. The parcels need two handfuls at quarter past nine, and she will fill all four.

main.title: Dinner in a Foil Parcel
materials: 4 potatoes, parboiled and cooled (adult, done the night before)
Green beans, zucchini, sweetcorn or whatever is in the fridge
steps: Tear four sheets of foil off the roll, each about the length of your forearm, and lay them flat on the tray and the table.
One cold potato into the middle of each sheet. She squashes it flat with the back of the tablespoon.
Load them together: a spoon of butter, a handful of grated cheese, her snapped beans, whatever else came out of the fridge.
Fold. Bring the two long edges up to meet, fold them over each other twice, then fold each end up twice. She brings the edges together and you pinch the seams shut.
Write a name on every parcel in marker. Hers, Kreston's, yours, Joseph's.
Back on the tray, into the fridge, and into a hot oven at half past five for thirty minutes.
main.tip: Shiny side in or out makes no difference. The seal does: a parcel folded flat at every edge steams the potato through, and one that gapes stays hard.

outside.title: Chalking the Shade
paras: Take the chalk out at half past ten and draw round the shadows: the tent, the fence post, the trash can, her own. Fat lines, and write the time inside one. Go back before dinner and find every shape sitting in the sun with its shadow moved. Bring the chalk out again for the redraw.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and carries things while he walks, so give him a fat piece of chalk and let him take it round the patio. He will not draw with it yet. He holds it, drops it, sits down on the line you chalked and slaps the ground flat-handed.

second.title: Rolling the Beds
second.intro: Four bedrolls, one per person, tied and labeled. They stay rolled by the tent door until Thursday.
materials: 1 blanket or large towel per person, four in total
String, cut into 8 lengths of eighteen inches
Thick card cut into 4 luggage labels
steps: Blanket flat on the floor, pillow across one end, both long sides folded in over it so the roll ends up the width of the pillow.
Roll from the pillow end, tight, kneeling on it as it goes to push the air out. She kneels, you roll, swap halfway.
Two ties on each roll, a third of the way in from each end, knotted twice. Her finger holds the first knot while you pull the second.
Punch a hole in the corner of each label. The punch is yours, or the scissors are, and they go back on the shelf after.
She names each roll and you write it on the label in marker, then thread the label onto one of the ties.
Stand all four on end by the tent door, then let her untie hers and lie down on it. Roll and tie it again together.
second.tip: Tie them tighter than feels kind. A roll that sags apart the first time she lifts it gets abandoned by dinner.

alternatives: One bedroll only, hers, and leave the other three.
Sleeping bags out of the loft instead, unrolled and lain on.
Pack a bag for the tent: one book, one teddy, one flashlight.
outAgain: The lakeshore, going late enough that the heat has come off the path
The duck pond, closer, if the drive is more than today can carry
A shaded woodland walk with the water bottles filled to the top
Home, the paddling pool, and nobody in the car at all
days.krestonPM: He walks now, and at the lakeshore he heads for the water without breaking stride, so he stays within arm's reach. Back at camp, hand him a folded towel to carry to the tent door and let him make the trip four times. At 13 months he would rather carry laundry than a toy.

insight.headline: Fever makes children clingy, and meeting it is the fastest way through the day.
paras: August is the month somebody in the house goes down with something. Azlyn will want to be on you all day once she is running a temperature, and she drops the independence she had last week. That is her nervous system spending its energy on the infection and borrowing regulation from you. A fever runs its own course whatever anybody does, so what sits in your hands is how the hours feel while it runs. Carrying her makes them shorter for both of you, and pushing her back into a normal day buys an argument you lose. Cancel the day, keep the fluids coming, and let her lie on you.

days.safety: The oven is on and the parcels come out hot and full of steam, which scalds worse than the tray does. You open them, away from both children, and let them stand two minutes first. At the lakeshore Kreston is 13 months and walks straight at water, so he is within arm's reach the whole time. The shadow chalking and the lakeshore are both open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors and the hole punch stay with you.

days.title: The Day Outside
days.prepTonight: Old blanket, cushions and sun hats by the back door, a full pitcher in the fridge, and the old shower curtain out for Monday.

opening.title: Carrying the Day Outside
opening.need: 1 laundry basket · the old blanket · 2 cushions.
steps: Hand her the basket at the back door and tell her the whole day is going outside and staying there.
She loads it and carries it out. Blanket first, then the cushions, then whatever else she decides the day needs. Two trips is fine and four is better.
Spread the blanket in the deepest shade in the yard and leave it. That is the floor until dinner.

main.title: Lying Down and Listening
materials: 1 pitcher of water and 3 lidded cups
1 paper bag for anything she picks up
steps: Blanket in full shade, cushions at one end, pitcher and cups where you can reach them lying down. Hats on before anybody lies back.
Round one, eight minutes, eyes shut. Take turns naming one thing you can hear. A bee, a car, a door, the leaves. The long silences are where the small sounds arrive, so let them run.
Round two, six minutes, eyes open and still flat on your back. Name what crosses the sky: a bird, a plane, a leaf going over, one cloud pushing past another.
Round three, six minutes, palms and heels down on the ground beside the blanket. Grass, a root, a stone, a dry crumbling patch, an ant on her ankle. Anything she wants to keep goes in the paper bag.
Pour a cup at every change of round whether she asks or not, and refill from the pitcher when it runs low.
Twenty minutes covers all three rounds, and the rest of the hour is hers. The blanket, the shade and the water stay where they are, and she uses them however she likes.
main.tip: You will want to fill the gaps. Sit in them. Count ten after each thing she names, and she fills the space herself.

outside.title: The Barefoot Lap
paras: Shoes and socks off at the back step, then walk the garden edge right round, twice. Grass in the shade, grass in the sun, the warm slab by the door, gravel, a drain cover, the cold patch under the tap. She names each one as she stands on it. The slab and the drain cover get the back of your hand first. Nobody puts shoes back on until lunch.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and has walked most of his miles on carpet. Grass moves under him and tickles, and it stops him dead for a minute before he commits. Take his shoes off and set him down on the edge of the blanket. Let him choose when he steps off.

second.title: What the Clouds Turned Into
second.intro: Today you write the sky down. She lies back for a cloud, then comes up on her elbows to watch it become a drawing, six sheets or two.
materials: 1 hardback book or stiff card as a drawing board
steps: Tape a sheet of paper to the book so the breeze cannot lift it, and sit beside her with the pencil and the board on your knees.

She lies back, calls a cloud and says what it is, then sits up next to you to watch it appear. You draw the thing she said rather than the thing you can see. A dog with eight legs is a dog with eight legs.
Write her words along the bottom of the sheet, the ones she used, then tape on a fresh page. Six sheets, six clouds.
Clip the finished pages to the corner of the blanket as they come off the board, or the first gust puts them over the fence.
Hand her the crayons and let her fill in the sky round each shape while the next cloud arrives.
On an empty blue afternoon she names what is moving instead: a bird, a plane, a bee, the top of the tree bending.
Sit her up with the stack and let her read all six to Kreston, page by page, in her own words rather than the ones written down.
second.tip: Draw a bad one and take your time over it. She corrects it, and the correcting tells you what she can see up there.

alternatives: One cloud, one page, and the hour loose on the blanket.
Color six sheets of sky blue and cut the shapes tomorrow.
Photograph six clouds and draw them indoors.
outAgain: A long walk with the stroller, after the heat and routed through shade
The riverside path, for the cool coming off the water
A shaded playground she has not seen since spring
Nowhere, and a second hour on the blanket
days.krestonPM: He goes in the stroller for the walk and out of it the moment there is grass. At 13 months he climbs every curb, every step and the low wall by the gate. Give him the wall for five minutes rather than lifting him past it. Water at every stop.

insight.headline: Naming a sound is how she learns to pick it out of the rest.
paras: Lying still and saying a bee looks like nothing and is hard work for her. A garden hands Azlyn one wash of noise, and to name a bee in it she holds that one thread and lets the traffic, the leaves and her own breathing fall to the back. Small children get better at this with practice, and the practice needs somewhere quiet enough for the small sounds to arrive, which is what the gaps are for. Attaching a word to a sound makes it a thing she can find again tomorrow. Eyes shut helps, because nothing else is competing for her.

days.safety: The whole day runs outdoors, so the sun comes first: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, blanket in full shade, water at every change of round. Walk the barefoot circuit yourself in shoes first and clear the glass, the dog mess and whatever the trash cans dropped. The paper bag of stones and grit stays up on the bench with you. Kreston is 13 months and puts everything he picks up into his mouth, so check his fists at every change of round and swap what you find for something too big to swallow.

days.title: Water at Camp
days.prepTonight: Two dishpans and a low bench out by the tent, the shower curtain and the swimsuits where you can find them at one o'clock, and fill the kettle.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Dish Towels Off the Line

opening.title: Everything That Needs Washing
steps: Send her round camp with the basket for every cup, plate and spoon used since Friday.
Wipe the worst off each one with the damp cloth at the back door, so nothing goes into the dishwashing with yesterday's cheese on it.
Count the cups out loud into the basket. That number is hers for the morning.

main.title: The Camp Dishwashing Station
materials: Warm water from the kettle, topped up cold
2 chairs to string the line between
The camp cups, plates and silverware
1 low bench, upturned crate or step
steps: Bench in the shade, two bowls side by side. Fill the left from the kettle and top it up cold until you can hold your hand in it. Fill the right one cold.
One squirt of dish soap into the left bowl only, and let her whisk up the foam with her arm in to the elbow.
Brush for the plates, sponge for the cups. Left bowl first, then straight into the right one to rinse. She does every piece and you re-do the two that matter.
Rinsed things stack on the bench to drip. She builds the stack.
String the short line between two chairs, hand her the six clothespins, and peg up the dish towel and whatever else got wet.
Tip both bowls out onto the grass the moment the last cup is done. She carries them in one at a time, empty.
main.tip: Give her the left bowl and keep the tap and the kettle to yourself. Stopping her to top it up ends the job.

outside.title: Water for the Birds
paras: Birds run short of water in early August. Stand a wide shallow dish or an upturned trash can lid in the shade, fill it a thumb deep, and put a flat stone in the middle for the smaller birds. She fills it, carries it and picks the spot.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and walks straight at water, so site the bird dish where you can see it. Give him his own, an inch in the bottom of a bucket and a cup, with you beside it. Pouring is the whole afternoon at his age, and he is never near it unsupervised.

second.title: The Soapy Slide
second.intro: A shower curtain, two buckets and a squirt of dish soap turn the lawn into the thing she talks about for two weeks.
materials: 1 old shower curtain, tarpaulin or heavy plastic sheet (two split trash bags taped together works for a short one)
4 heavy stones or tent pegs for the corners
steps: Walk the patch first with your hand and then your bare foot, feeling for stones and buried roots before anything goes down.
Lay the sheet flat on level grass, well clear of the path, the step and the fence posts, and weight all four corners with the stones.
Tip the first bucket down it from the top end, add the squirt of dish soap halfway along, and spread it with your hand.
Swimsuits on. Show her the run-up once: three steps and sit down, feet first, head up. Sitting is the only landing.
Second bucket over it whenever the middle goes dry, about every ten minutes in this heat.
Stop before she is finished rather than after. Straight into a warm towel, and the swimsuit comes off out on the grass.
Roll the sheet up away from the tent and stand it in the shade to dry.
second.tip: More water and less soap. A second squirt turns the grass round the sheet into a skating rink for whoever walks past holding Kreston.

alternatives: The paddling pool with the dishpans in it.
Wash the bikes and the trike with the leftover foam.
Water fights with two cups and a bucket, no sheet.
outAgain: The duck pond, going late and taking rolled oats rather than bread
The riverside path for the shade and the breeze off the water
The splash pad, if there is one within a sensible drive
The garden again, with the sprinkler on low
days.krestonPM: He stays off the sheet. A 13-month-old on wet plastic goes down backwards and hits his head, so he gets the grass beside it and a bucket with an inch in it. At the pond he will walk in, so he holds a hand or he goes in the stroller.

insight.headline: Summer needs less structure than you'd think.
paras: This week has a plan on every page, and the days that land best are the ones where you follow half of it. Long stretches of unbroken outdoor time do what a sequence of good activities cannot: she gets bored, stays bored, and then invents. The gap between running out of ideas and finding one is where her own play comes from, and an adult who fills it with a suggestion closes it. Children with long free afternoons build longer, more complicated play than those on a run of planned blocks. Put the water out and let the afternoon go where she takes it.

days.safety: Run your hand over the whole patch before the sheet goes down. A stone or a buried root under wet plastic is what turns a slide into a hospital trip. Lay it on flat grass, never near a path, a step or a fence post. Keep Kreston off the sheet and out of the bowls, and stay within arm's reach of him the whole time either bowl holds water. A 13-month-old drowns in the depth of a dishpan, so tip both out the moment you finish. Soap and water take the cream straight off, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, and again before the sheet goes down.

days.title: The Camp Flag
days.prepTonight: Old white pillowcase, three paints, the wide brush and newspaper on the table, and the garden cane by the back door with the swim bag.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Sign Hunt Down to the Pool

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Swim Bag by the Door

opening.title: What Our Camp Is Called
steps: Sit in the tent and ask what camp is called. Take the first answer, however daft, and say it back with camp in front of it.
Ask what one picture would stand for it. A sun, a fish, a boat, the letter K. She picks.
She draws it small five or six times while you watch. The fifth one goes on the flag at quarter past nine.

main.title: The Flag Over the Tent
materials: 1 old white pillowcase, dish towel or plain t-shirt
1 garden cane, bamboo pole, broom handle or a long straight stick
1 jar of water and a wet washcloth
steps: Push a ball of masking tape onto the top end of the cane before you carry it out to her. Then newspaper down in the shade, pillowcase flat on top, and slide two more sheets inside it so the paint cannot come through to the back.
Her drawing goes beside it as the reference. One symbol, and it wants to fill most of the cloth.
Paint. The brush is wide on purpose and the jar of water sits between the three colors. The washcloth comes to her, not her to the tap.
Leave it flat in the sun, which in this heat dries it in twenty minutes.
Cut two short pieces off the string and tape a loop to each top corner of the flag. Nothing gets taped to the cane, because the flag has to travel up and down it this afternoon.
Lash the pole to the fence post by the tent door with the rest of the string.
main.tip: One symbol, and big. A flag with six things on it reads as a smudge from the other end of the garden.

outside.title: The Sign Hunt Down to the Pool
paras: Walk the route you take to swimming and count the signs: the red circle that means stop, the stick figure that means children, the arrow, the triangle on the recycling bin. She spots them and you say what each tells somebody who cannot read. Turn at the pool gates and walk back.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and walks, so let him do the first stretch on his feet with a finger to hold, then into the stroller. He points with his whole arm. Name the sign out loud when he aims at one, and keep walking.

second.title: Flag Up, Flag Down
second.intro: Three signals, two chalked stations and a bell. She runs the messages between them.
materials: 2 clothespins to hold the flag at half height
Chalk to mark the two stations
1 saucepan lid and 1 wooden spoon as the camp bell
steps: Chalk two circles twenty of her steps apart, camp at one end and the gate at the other.
Agree three signals and no more. Flag at the top means come to camp, flag halfway means camp is shut, flag waved means dinner.

Knot one end of the six-foot string through both corner loops, run it up over the taped ball on the end of the pole and down the far side, and pull the loose end to send the flag to the top. The two pegs pinch the string against the pole to hold it at half height for shut.
She stands in the gate circle with her back to camp. One bang on the saucepan lid with the wooden spoon means look at the flag. She turns, reads it, does it.
Swap. She works the string and the bell while you stand at the gate, and get it wrong on purpose twice so she has to correct you.
Hand out the two dish towels as hand flags and send messages across the yard with nobody speaking, including you. Leave the flag at the top when you go swimming.
second.tip: Three signals is the ceiling. Add a fourth and the whole thing turns into guessing.

alternatives: Flag up and flag down only, and drop the bell.
Paint a second small flag for Kreston's stroller.
Chalk the three signals on the path as pictures instead.
outAgain: Swimming, and the flag left flying at home
The splash pad, if the pool session is full
The paddling pool and the hose in the yard
A cool bath and a shady afternoon, if nobody can face the drive
days.krestonPM: He is 13 months and will go into the water off the side without checking whether anyone has hold of him. Arm's reach means the tiles as well as the water. Twenty-five minutes is plenty. Hold him under the arms and walk him along the shallow end so he does the stepping.

insight.headline: Symbols are a big abstraction, and flags are the easiest entry point.
paras: The painted sun on that pillowcase is a mark standing in for an idea, which is the same trick as a letter standing in for a sound, and letters are eighteen months away. Azlyn can hold the flag version now because it is one picture with one meaning, chosen by her and visible from across the yard. Raising and lowering it adds a second layer: the same object saying two different things depending on where it sits. Every road sign she named this morning runs on that rule. She is doing the groundwork for reading in a form she can pick up and wave.

days.safety: A garden cane ends at the height of a running three-year-old's eye, so push the ball of masking tape onto the top end before the cane comes out to her, and lash the pole to the fence post so it cannot topple. Kreston is 13 months and will go into the pool without warning, so he is within arm's reach on the tiles and in the water. Painting and signal drills both run in the open: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you, and the string comes off the pole at bedtime.

days.title: The Day Before
days.prepTonight: Cut twelve strips out of thick card, a hand long each, and stand them on the table with the crayons. Put one bag per person by the front door and check the flashlight batteries.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Four Bags by the Door

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Early Bath, Bag by the Door

opening.title: One Bag Each
opening.need: 1 rucksack or tote bag per person, four in all.
steps: Lay the four bags open in a row on the floor and let her hand them out. Hers, Kreston's, yours, Joseph's.
Ask her what goes in each one and write nothing down. Let the list be as wrong as she makes it.
Tell her the drawings start at quarter past nine and nothing goes in a bag until it has been drawn.

main.title: The Picture Packing List
materials: 1 rucksack or tote bag per person, four in all
The things still indoors: the flashlight, the cups, the sun hats, the water bottles, the sun cream
steps: Twelve strips in a row on the table. Name twelve things that have to go out to camp in the morning and let her do the naming, with you holding back the two she forgets.
She draws one thing on each strip in crayon. A flashlight is a rectangle with lines coming out of it.
You write the word underneath each drawing in marker, so anybody in the house can read her list.
Loop a piece of masking tape onto the back of every strip and stick the row along the wall at her height, in the order things go into the bags.
Fetch each thing off the shelf and pack against her list. She pulls a strip off the wall and lays it face down as each thing goes in.
When the last strip is face down, clip all twelve together with the bulldog clip and hang it on her bag for the morning.
main.tip: Let her pack her own bag and leave what she puts in it alone. A rucksack holding two teddies and one cup is one she carries the whole way tomorrow.

outside.title: Where Everything Goes Tomorrow
paras: Walk out to the tent after the snack and stand in the doorway with her. She settles four things. The shade at eleven and the shade at three. The side of the door the water bowl stands on. The spot for the bench, set so nobody carries a full pitcher past the fire. The first thing out of the bags in the morning. You write none of it down, because she will remember.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and carries things while he walks, so give him one plastic cup and the job of getting it out to the tent door and back. He will take a route nobody else would choose. He understands bring it here about half the time.

second.title: The Camp Snack Bags
second.intro: You make tomorrow's food this afternoon. Four tubs, three things in each, and she scoops and counts.
materials: 4 small tubs or clean jam jars with lids
Chopped dried apricot or dried apple
steps: Tray on the table, four tubs in a row along it with the lids off and set aside.
Cereal hoops first. One cup into each tub, and she levels the top of the cup off with her finger before it goes in.
One tablespoon of raisins into each. She counts the spoons out loud and starts again if she loses count.
One tablespoon of the chopped apricot into each, counted the same way.
Lids on, and she presses every one until it clicks. Any tub that will not shut gets a spoonful taken back out.
A sticky label on each lid. She writes her own name on hers however it comes out and you write the other three while she watches.
Line all four up by the bags at the door. Kreston's is the one you chop into in the morning, not now.
second.tip: Let her spill. A tray under the whole operation turns three spilt spoonfuls into something she tips back into the tub herself.

alternatives: One tub, hers, and the rest done after she is in bed.
Bake oat bars for tomorrow instead and cut them into four.
Sort a bag of raisins into four piles by eye, then check them with a spoon.
outAgain: The library, and ask at the desk for anything about tents or the woods at night
Indoor playground, if the library is full of the holiday crowd
The park with the big trees, and a book each under one
The store for tomorrow's bread, and she carries it
days.krestonPM: Take him to the library and let him walk in on his own feet, which takes four minutes. At 13 months he pulls board books off the low shelf faster than anyone can put them back, so sit on the floor and let that shelf be his. Azlyn picks his book and carries it to the desk.

insight.headline: A list she can read herself puts her in charge of the packing.
paras: Twelve cards on the wall do a job Azlyn cannot do in her head yet. She can hold two or three steps at a time, and camp needs twelve, so the row of drawings carries the order for her and leaves her hands and her attention free for the packing itself. Turning each card face down as the thing goes in the bag is the part that earns its keep: she checks her own work and knows where she has got to without asking you. Small children finish more of a long task on their own from a list they can see than from the same list said out loud. She drew these, so they are hers to run.

days.safety: Raisins, dried apricot and cereal hoops are all the wrong size for a 13-month-old, so Kreston's portion gets chopped small in the morning and he does not get near the open tubs today. Loose food bags and plastic wrap go straight into the trash, not onto the floor where he is working. The planning stand at the tent door is twenty minutes of open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Big Camp Out
days.prepTonight: Bags packed by the door, water bottles filled and in the fridge, and the sun cream and both hats on top of the pile.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Whole Camp in One Place

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Shady Loop Back to Camp

opening.title: Everything in Three Trips
opening.need: the four packed bags · 2 laundry baskets.
steps: Load the two baskets with everything the bags could not take.
Three trips out to the tent and no more. Count them out loud.
Put it all down in one heap on the grass beside the door. The rest of camp goes on at quarter past nine.

main.title: The Whole Camp in One Place
materials: The paper campfire and its ring of stones
steps: Hats on before anything else. Walk the tent with her first, both sides: every peg along the line, all four corner ties, every stone on the hem. She finds what a week of wind has shifted and puts it back, and a spare peg goes in wherever one has blown off.
Six fresh stones along the two long edges from the outside, spaced so the walls hang straight. She knows this part and will tell you where you have it wrong.
Rug down inside and wiped over with the damp cloth, then the four bedrolls along the back wall in the order she decides, labels facing out.
Fire ring straightened out front, sticks stacked back into their tripod, any paper flame that has come off taped back on.

Flag to the top of the pole, because camp is open. Then the cups, the snack tubs and the flashlight out of the bags and into the tent where she wants them, his tub chopped smaller than his fingernail first.
Dishpan down at the tent door with the pitcher beside it. Then stand at the gate with her and look at the whole thing from thirty feet.
main.tip: Move the rug rather than the tent. Shade crosses the floor by noon, and shifting what she sits on takes a minute where the sheet takes the morning.

outside.title: The Shady Loop Back to Camp
paras: Out early and short. Take the route that stays under trees, fill the bottles before you leave, and turn for home before eleven. Look for what else is sheltering: the dog under the bench, birds deep in the hedge, nobody on the field. Come back in through the front of the tent.

days.infant: Kreston turns 14 months today. He stacks two blocks now, so give him two of the fire stones, each wider than his fist, and let him try to put one on the other beside the ring. He has three to five words and one of them will come out today. Say happy fourteen months out loud to him, because nobody else is going to.

second.title: Striking Camp
second.intro: Camp comes down on purpose, while everybody still likes it, in the order it went up.
materials: 1 dustpan and brush, or a stiff yard broom
Your phone, for the photograph before it comes down
steps: Photograph it full first, with both of them inside it, before one thing moves. Take more than you need and take one from the gate.
Flag down off the pole and she folds it corner to corner twice. The pole comes off the post and lies flat on the grass.
Pegs off the line into the peg bag, six at a time so she can count them, then the sheet down and shaken.
Bedrolls stay tied and go into the baskets with the rug on top.
Carry the fire sticks back to the hedge they came from and tip them under it. The stones go back along the wall in a line.
Wipe the bowl and the cups out with the damp cloth and carry them in.
Sweep the ground flat until you cannot tell camp was there. She does the last of it on her own, then walks the empty patch.
second.tip: Strike it an hour before anybody has had enough. Taking it down while it is still good is what makes her willing to put it up again.

alternatives: Leave the tent standing and take down everything else.
Photograph camp from six angles and print two.
Move the whole camp four feet to the left instead.
outAgain: The bakery, and she carries the bag home flat in both hands
The corner store for something cold, walked to and eaten on the step
The library again, for the cool air as much as the books
The duck pond in the last of the shade
days.krestonPM: At 14 months he wants to carry whatever everybody else is carrying, so give him the empty peg bag for the walk to the bakery. Your hand on the back of his neck says whether you keep going.

insight.headline: Big days are frequently too big, and the fix is leaving early.
paras: The whole camp is up, everyone is enjoying it, and the temptation is to stay until somebody falls apart. Leave while it is still good instead, at the point where she would take another twenty minutes without argument. Small children remember the end of an experience out of all proportion to the rest, so an hour that finished well outranks three hours that ended in the grass screaming. You have watched this from the other side at every party she has ever been carried home from. Cutting a good day short by an hour is what makes her ask for the same thing again.

days.safety: A whole day outdoors in the first week of August is a sun day before it is a heat day: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, and once more after lunch. Shade over camp by eleven, and water every half hour. Kreston is 14 months and cannot tell you he is overheating, so watch for a hot dry neck, a red face and a sudden flop, and take him indoors to cool down. The dishpan at the tent door holds water only while somebody washes in it: stay within arm's reach of him while it stands full and tip it out over the grass the moment you finish. Raisins, cereal hoops and dried apricot are throat-sized at 14 months, so his tub gets chopped in the kitchen and the other three stay off the tent floor. Every stone you hand him is wider than his fist.
